title: Accara, Black-Eyed Pea Fritters
author: SAVEUR (May 2012 print issue)
desc: A cup of dried black-eyed peas soaked at least eight hours, skinned, puréed with baking soda and a quarter of an onion, and fried by the tablespoon at 365° for about three minutes.
longDesc: The Saveur printing is the most procedural accara in the set. The peas soak in cold water in the fridge for eight hours or overnight, are pulsed about eight times in a food processor to loosen the skins, covered with water and rubbed between the palms until the skins float to the top, and drained; the washing is repeated until the skins are gone. The skinless peas are puréed with baking soda, a quarter of a small onion, salt, pepper and three tablespoons of water until smooth, then dropped by the tablespoon into oil at 365° and fried about three minutes. They are salted straight from the oil and served with kaani sauce. The recipe makes about 30 fritters.
ingredients: 3 tbsp water — appears only in the method
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper — quantities not printed
Canola oil for frying — oil to a depth of 2 inches
steps: Cover the peas with cold water by 2 inches in a large container, cover and refrigerate at least 8 hours or overnight.

Drain the peas and pulse them in the food processor about 8 times, until slightly broken and the skins separate. Put them in a bowl, cover with water and rub between the palms to loosen the skins. Let sit until the skins float to the top, then slowly drain off the skins. Add more water and repeat until all the skins are gone.
Put the skinless peas in a blender with the baking soda, onion, salt, pepper and 3 tablespoons of water. Purée until smooth, scraping down the sides.
Pour oil to a depth of 2 inches into a 6-quart Dutch oven and heat over medium-high until a deep-fry thermometer reads 365° (unit not printed).

Working in batches, drop tablespoon-sized balls of batter into the oil with two small spoons and cook about 3 minutes, until golden brown. Drain on paper towels and sprinkle with salt. Serve with kaani sauce.
chefTips: The skins float — that is the printed cue for when a rinse is finished.
Purée until completely smooth; a gritty batter fries unevenly.
Season the fritters with salt straight from the oil.
commonMistakes: Leaving skins in — the fritters turn grey and bitter.
Dropping batter into oil that is not up to temperature, so it soaks oil.
Over-large spoonfuls: the printed size is a tablespoon.
reheating: Recrisp in a hot oven for 5 to 8 minutes.
healthBenefits: Black-eyed peas supply plant protein and fibre.
Frying adds fat; the fritters are a snack, not a daily food.
culturalNote: Accara is eaten at breakfast and as a street snack across Senegal. The au-senegal.com printing starts from ‘farine de niébé fermenté’ — fermented black-eyed pea flour — with no method for making it, so the fermentation is outsourced and undocumented; this Saveur printing is from soaked whole peas with no ferment.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Accara (Black-Eyed Pea Fritters)’. Byline status: magazine, no individual author (SAVEUR, May 2012 feature by John O’Connor). Published online 22 May 2012. Yield ‘makes 30 fritters’; ‘Serves’ field has no number. SINGLE-PASS.

Printed temperature: 365° — unit not printed. Cues in fragments: ‘the peas are slightly broken and the skins separate’; ‘the skins float to the top’; ‘smooth’; ‘golden brown’. Soak ‘at least 8 hours or overnight’ — time stated, no endpoint; this is a soak, not a ferment.
ABSENT, not estimated: salt and pepper amounts; the oil quantity beyond the 2-inch depth.

Also recorded and not published: au-senegal.com’s ‘Recette des accras de niébé’ (byline ‘le cœur du Sénégal’, 2014, modified 2023) — starts from bought fermented black-eyed pea flour; its step 5 says to cook the balls ‘dans l’eau chaude’ immediately after step 4 heats the oil (near-certainly ‘l’huile’, reported as printed and not fixed); batter rest ‘laisser reposer 30 mn’ is time only; no frying temperature or time. Held as unpublishable.
